edition.note: JOIM review cites "Kindle Edition (April 20, 2015)"; Investing by the Books lists The Idea Farm, 2015. Self-published, about 130 pages; no later or revised edition found. Reviews describe 13 chapters plus appendices, which the three Lessons follow.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils the opening chapters: the history of stocks, bonds and bills, and the famous portfolios Faber lines up. It matters because your €40k needs one mix, and this is the menu.
rows.note: JOIM review (Estrada, 2016): "Faber starts off with a brief discussion of the long-term performance of stocks, bonds, and bills", then the benchmark and the named investors' portfolios. The EUR 40k figure is the reader's own, not a book claim.

rows.claim: The benchmark is the classic 60/40: 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds. Faber also tests a global version that spreads both parts across the world's markets.
rows.note: Review lists "Classic 60/40: 60% S&P 500, 40% 10-year US Treasuries" and a Global 60/40 with stocks and bonds each split 50/50 US/foreign. JOIM review calls 60-40 the benchmark portfolio.

rows.claim: Ray Dalio's All Seasons portfolio, made public through Tony Robbins, holds 30 percent stocks, 55 percent medium and long-term bonds, and 15 percent gold and commodities.
rows.note: Irish Times on the book: Dalio portfolio holds 30% stocks, 55% in 10- and 30-year bonds, the rest in gold and commodities. MoneySense (https://www.moneysense.ca/columns/raining-on-the-all-seasons-portfolio/) gives 30/40/15/7.5/7.5 and says it was publicised in Tony Robbins' Money: Master the Game.

rows.claim: The Ivy's five parts, 20 percent each, are US stocks, foreign stocks, bonds, real estate trusts (REITs) and commodities.
rows.note: Secondary: Ivy Portfolio (Faber) is 20% each in US large-cap stocks, developed ex-US stocks, US intermediate Treasuries, US REITs and commodities. The passage in Global Asset Allocation itself was not opened.

rows.claim: Faber also tests the mixes of well-known investors, such as Warren Buffett's suggested 90 percent stocks and 10 percent short-term government bonds.
rows.note: Buffett 2013 letter as quoted: "Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund." Irish Times confirms the book tests Buffett 90/10.

rows.claim: Faber runs every portfolio on the same data from 1973 to 2013 and reports returns after inflation, so the comparison is fair.
rows.note: Irish Times reports the book's real (after-inflation) annualised returns since 1973; JOIM review and mymoneyblog give the comparison period as 1973-2013. JOIM also mentions asset data from 1970.

rows.claim: He also warns that 1973 to 2013 included a long fall in interest rates, which gave bonds unusually strong returns that may not repeat.
rows.note: No opened source shows Faber warning that falling interest rates over 1973-2013 flattered bonds. What is confirmed: the book cites "very low yields in the bond market" and expects about 2.2% nominal from bonds over the next ten years. Card and Check b09c1l2k3 (prompt, fare, correct option) reworded to that.

rows.claim: For you, a 70/30 versus an 80/20 split is a small choice by Faber's measure. His result says cost and staying with the plan matter more than the exact split.
rows.note: JOIM quotes the book: "Fees are far more important than your asset allocation decision!" and says investors should choose an allocation and stick with it. The 70/30 and 80/20 splits are the reader's own example.

rows.claim: Faber shows that an advisor charging around 1 percent a year, plus fund fees, can turn the best allocation into one of the worst.
rows.note: Faber interview: mutual funds average 1.25 percent a year and an adviser "on average, charges 1 percent a year". mymoneyblog quotes the book: advisory fees transform "the BEST performing asset allocation into lower than the WORST".

rows.claim: When you compare Interactive Brokers and DEGIRO, add up ten years of trading, custody and fund costs, then learn how Box 3 taxes what you hold.
rows.note: Application card, no book claim. Belastingdienst confirms Box 3 taxes a notional return on savings and investments. The ten-year horizon is the app's own exercise.

rows.claim: Your 80 percent index core follows Faber's rule: start near the global market, keep costs low and stick with it while the satellites take the risks.
rows.note: No opened source confirms "start near the global market" as Faber's rule. Reworded to what the JOIM review confirms: a global mix, low costs, stick with it. The 80 percent core is the reader's own figure. Unlisted card b09c1l3p3 makes the same starting-point claim and was left as is.

rows.claim: Faber treats it as the natural starting point: it needs no forecasts, because its weights are simply what the world's investors already hold.
rows.note: Not a listed Card. No source confirmed that Faber calls the global market portfolio "the natural starting point"; the attribution was removed and the description of the portfolio kept.
